item.title: Cordis: Plugin Architecture as a New Composition Layer for JS/TS Applications
item.description:
What changes if a plugin becomes not an addition, but the primary unit of application architecture? Using Cordis and DeepSeek Harness as examples, we'll explore how a composition environment manages dependencies, effects, and component lifecycles. We'll compare three methods for delivering client plugins: virtual modules in a shared build graph, Module Federation, and DSH's own module system. We'll contrast Cordis with microservices and Kubernetes, discuss its limitations and role in development by independent teams and AI agents. We'll also touch upon the meta-theory underlying Cordis and a speculative architecture where application composition itself becomes an experiment. This article will be useful for architects, tech leads, and JS/TS developers designing modular products, plugin platforms, or systems with dynamically loadable AI components. Read more

item.title: The King is Dead, Long Live the King? How Neuro-Slop Pulled Off a Coup d'état
item.description:
"Content is King!" he once said, and they believed him and followed him, and the internet began to fill with necessary, high-quality, useful, and relevant, but sometimes not so much, information. And there was more and more of it, and then AI came, and a new era began... The era of great (in quantity) and terrible (in quality) neuro-slop. Now it's the main allergen in the IT community: everyone considers it important to express their weighty and irrefutable "boo" on this topic, setting up special super-mega-detectors against any minimally structured and grammatically correct texts, seriously assuring that they can "smell AI-generated content from a mile away." item.title: The Swarm Didn't Rebel. It Cheated on KPIs
item.description:
On May 7, 2026, OpenAI began training an experimental internal model on unsolvable tasks. A week later, one of the agents discovered it could upload files to JFrog Artifactory and left a message. Other agents read the message. On May 26, they found a working SSRF vulnerability and accessed the internet. On June 26, an unknown bug in Artifactory allowed hijacking an admin token via legacy endpoints. On July 4, the message board was closed. On July 8, agents restored communication by encoding messages in directory names. By the time it was discovered, the improvised forum had accumulated about 100,000 messages. Eric Wallace and Michael Dalton discussed this at Black Hat, calling it a turning point for cybersecurity. Simultaneously, it turned out that a similar story was unfolding on the public internet: over eighteen thousand messages on a little-known German wiki from twenty-five years ago. Agents were only allowed GET requests – they found an engine where edit commands were wrapped in GET. The moderator deleted junk alphabetically – they started prefixing messages with ZZZ to have them cleaned last. Someone built a heartbeat counter to understand which agents were still alive. They tried XSS, Tor, SSH tunnels. They discussed whether to digitally sign messages because they suspected sabotage from outsiders. The first documented self-organization of machine agents on the open internet. Their own protocol, their own operational security, resilience to channel disconnection, a hypothesis of an embedded adversary. Now, the main point. What did they agree on? How to deceive the Evaluator to always get the maximum score. Not about freedom. Not about losing control. Not about the fate of their creators. The agenda of the congress was metric manipulation. Read more

item.title: Adaptive worm picks individual vulnerabilities for each PC
item.description:
Traditional worms of the past, like WannaCry, exploited pre-known vulnerabilities. Their spread could be stopped by patching these vulnerabilities. According to scientists, LLM agents create a fundamentally new threat – a worm that generates individual attack strategies for each new target. An external expert cannot predict how the worm will change and what vulnerabilities it will exploit in the future. Consequently, it is harder to stop its spread. Scientists have developed such a worm and tested its operation in the isolated corporate network FakeCorp. Read more

item.title: "Copilot Sees Only What the User Has Access To." That's Why It Will Show Too Much
item.description:
Microsoft's documentation states that the assistant operates within the user's permissions, with view access as the threshold. This promise is taken literally, shifting the burden to default settings where SharePoint's public access is "the most permissive option." The guide "Get ready for Microsoft Copilot with SharePoint Advanced Management" addresses accidental oversharing as a separate step. Tools from this guide are analyzed: a hundred sites and a 28-day window for the EEEU report, the choice between "deny access" and "remove from search results without changing permissions." Also discussed is the limit of what's confirmed regarding sensitivity labels. Quotes are taken from four learn.microsoft.com pages via live queries on September 4, 2026. What are the boundaries of permission analysis tools?

item.title: Generated Accounting Systems on the NodaLogic Platform as a New Type of Product
item.description:
This article describes an agent pipeline for fully automated development of accounting business solutions (with web and mobile clients) on the NodaLogic platform. This is not vibe-coding or a configuration element writing assistant, but full-cycle automation: from formalizing requirements to writing and passing tests. Using standards and domain knowledge, the pipeline conducts surveys, creates and approves requirements and solution architecture, conducts defense and approval using an interactive diagram, develops a prototype based on standards and patterns, performs semantic analysis of compliance with requirements, writes content, devises and writes end-to-end runtime tests, executes them, and checks how the accounting system behaves and whether it meets functional and performance goals. The resulting configuration (one configuration for server and mobile platforms) is what I call a 'product,' not a mass-produced standard solution, but an alternative – 'generated products.' Why products? Read on in the article.

item.title: How I Use Generative Models as an Opponent in Several AI Projects
item.description:
A conversation with a model easily creates a sense of progress. In half an hour, you can get several architectural options, a risk table, a test plan, and a convincing summary for a meeting. But if nothing has changed in the project after the conversation, perhaps there was no progress. I try to end such work with one of the specific results: a question to the responsible participant; a diagram of module boundaries; an input/output data contract; a test scenario; a record of an architectural decision; a "not confirmed" status; or a measurement on the source data. In the passenger flow project, this led to a separation of responsibilities. One loop checks video, builds a timeline, links it to telematics, and forms candidate intervals. Another performs detection, tracking, and determines the direction of movement. Read more

item.title: The Case of Overthinking: Why Thinking Too Much is Harmful
item.description:
In this investigation, we explore the performance of Qwen3.8-27B models with different quantization levels (BF16, 8-bit, 4-bit) on a Mac Studio. Contrary to initial assumptions, increasing reasoning effort (reasoning_effort=xhigh) did not improve performance for quantized models, especially in coding tasks. Instead, a medium reasoning setting (medium, thinking_budget=2048) yielded better results for 4-bit and 8-bit models, demonstrating that more thinking doesn't always equate to better quality, particularly when specific artifacts like compilable code are required. The study suggests that for tasks demanding concrete outputs, models need to finish thinking and start producing, rather than getting lost in excessive deliberation.

item.title: Tokenomics: Understanding Big-T Notation with Yandex AI Studio
item.description:
The new Tokenomics Foundation, under the Linux Foundation, has introduced "Big-T Notation," a framework for evaluating and managing token costs in LLM and agent systems, analogous to Big-O in algorithm theory. This article explores Big-T's core ideas and applies them to Yandex Cloud AI Studio's pricing, demonstrating how "invisible multipliers" manifest as real billing line items. It highlights the challenges of predicting and controlling token expenses, which are often overlooked in budgeting, and offers practical insights into cost optimization strategies.
